primitives.description: External call re-enters mutable state before the original operation is safely finalized.
A re-entrant read observes transient state and influences an external consumer.
A callback-capable integration re-enters target logic during an in-flight operation.
Attacker-controlled market activity distorts a price used by protocol logic.
An oracle input, source, window, or dependency is manipulable or incorrectly trusted.
Atomic temporary liquidity enables otherwise capital-intensive state manipulation.
Assets are transferred directly outside the intended accounting entrypoint.
Share or exchange rate can be increased in a way that yields attacker-favorable conversions.
Initial low-supply state permits disproportionate influence over share conversion.
Integer rounding direction or order creates exploitable value transfer.
Insufficient numeric precision accumulates or exposes attacker-capturable discrepancy.
Two accounting representations diverge and protocol actions consume inconsistent state.
Raw token balance is incorrectly treated as equivalent to protocol-accounted assets.
Reward index state can be manipulated to misattribute or overclaim rewards.
Delayed or missing checkpointing causes actions to consume stale accounting state.
Sensitive behavior is callable by an unauthorized principal.
A principal can acquire or exercise a stronger role than intended.
Initialization state or authority can be seized, repeated, or misconfigured.
Upgrade authority or upgrade mechanics violate intended trust/security assumptions.
Proxy implementation/admin/beacon configuration permits unintended control or behavior.
A valid signature can be reused outside its intended nonce/domain/context.
Permit-style authorization can be replayed, forged, mis-scoped, or otherwise abused.
Token approvals or allowance transitions expose unintended transfer authority.
Attacker can influence an external call target/data/value beyond intended constraints.
Delegatecall target or context control can execute unintended code in caller storage.
Token transfer/mint/burn callback semantics create unexpected control flow.
Transferred amount differs from requested amount due to token-side fee mechanics.
Token balances change independently of explicit transfers and can desynchronize accounting.
ERC777 hooks create callback/reentrancy behavior across token operations.
ERC4626 conversion/preview/rounding or empty-vault edge behavior violates expectations.
Borrower state can avoid or distort intended liquidation conditions.
Accounting permits positions or system state to violate solvency constraints.
Collateral value, amount, or accounting can be manipulated to alter credit capacity.
Loss allocation or bad-debt handling transfers unintended losses to other participants.
Incorrect token/index orientation causes swaps, quotes, or accounting to use the wrong asset direction.
Execution lacks effective output/price protection or applies protection to the wrong quantity.
State-dependent action can be profitably bracketed or manipulated around execution.
Voting or governance control can be accumulated or exercised contrary to intended security assumptions.
Temporary borrowed voting power can influence governance within the relevant snapshot/execution window.
Cross-chain message origin, ordering, verification, or delivery assumptions are unsafe.
A valid action/message can be repeated in another accepted context.
System assumes finality or canonical ordering stronger than the underlying environment guarantees.
Required keeper execution can fail, be delayed, censored, or leave unsafe state.
Security/liveness depends on off-chain automation assumptions not enforced on-chain.
Attacker can prevent required protocol actions or render a critical path unusable.
Attacker can force excessive or unbounded gas cost to disrupt critical operations.
Storage layout incompatibility causes state corruption or privilege/value misinterpretation.
Security assumption depends on code identity/lifetime that can change or disappear.
External contract, oracle, token, bridge, or service failure invalidates protocol assumptions.
